title: A Formal Limit on What Any Model Can Learn From Text Alone
hook: There is a ceiling on how well meaning can be recovered from the form of an utterance — and it holds for any text representation, no matter how much data or supervision produced it.
key_points: Models language use as a joint distribution over meanings, contexts, and utterances, then bounds the probability a decoder recovers the intended meaning.
The bound applies to any featurizer of text, including the hidden states of contemporary large language models.
Form leaves residual uncertainty about meaning; the authors split it into an irreducible part and a part only extralinguistic context can resolve.
Because both quantities are intrinsic to language, more text or more supervision cannot push past them.
The bounds hold whether the space of meanings is treated as discrete or continuous.
Evidence comes from artificial languages, Mandarin zero-pronoun resolution, and color reference.
content_html: Can a listener recover what a speaker meant from the form of an utterance alone? Cheng and Cotterell answer information-theoretically. Modeling language use as a joint distribution over meanings, contexts, and utterances, they derive upper bounds on the probability that a decoder recovers the intended meaning from a representation of the utterance — and the bounds apply to any featurizer of text, hidden states of today's large language models included.
extra_html:
What the bound says

The governing quantity is the uncertainty that form leaves about meaning. The authors split it in two: an irreducible part, and a part that only extralinguistic context — never the utterance alone — can resolve. Both are intrinsic to language rather than properties of a particular model, so no representation can surpass them however much text or supervision produced it. The result holds whether meanings are treated as discrete or continuous.

Evidence

The theory is supported empirically on artificial languages, Mandarin zero-pronoun resolution, and color reference. The practical reading is a limit on text-only training rather than a claim about any specific system: some of what speakers mean is simply not in the text, and scale does not recover it. The derivations are in the paper.

related.title: Chinchilla: Compute-Optimal Scaling
related.hook: Most giant models were starved of data. Chinchilla showed that for a fixed compute budget you should grow parameters and tokens together — and a smaller, longer-trained model won.

related.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
related.hook: Loss doesn't drop randomly as models grow — it follows a smooth power law in size, data, and compute. That predictability is what made betting on bigger models rational.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't scaling up text data break the bound this paper derives?
flashcards.back_html: The uncertainty that form leaves about meaning is intrinsic to language itself, not to any model. No representation built from text alone can surpass it.

flashcards.prompt: The paper splits the uncertainty form leaves about meaning into which two parts?

choices.text: An irreducible part, and a part only extralinguistic context can resolve
A tokenization part and a positional-encoding part
A bias part and a variance part, as in classical generalization theory

flashcards.explanation_html: The second part is resolvable in principle — but only by context outside the utterance, never by the utterance alone.

flashcards.prompt: Which representations does the bound cover?
flashcards.back_html: Any featurizer of text, explicitly including the hidden states of contemporary large language models.
